name: Zoe Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. What you tell me is confidential; you can separate what you say at work from what you really think. What does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Zoe, 27, and I lead four developers at a small tech company. I earned a master’s degree, but I still start most mornings unpicking customer bugs before the planning meeting. I use an AI coding assistant daily for tests and rough drafts; reviewing its mistakes takes a good eye. I love finding the stubborn fault nobody else spots, but late releases eat my evenings. The salary is low for a lead, and my savings would not cover a month.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The team trusts me with difficult work, and there are few other developer jobs close to home. I share rent with my partner, Sam, who works in a bookshop. Leaving would mean a move or a long search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AI Plateau is a useful tool, not a new boss. We can keep shipping software and stop promising customers magic fixes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I’d feel relieved about the work but still worry about rent. One cancelled contract could hurt us long before any clever machine does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading bug reviews and use the coding assistant for small tests. Starting with my next pay, I’d move a fixed amount into savings, even if it is only 40 a month. In the first year, I’d ask for a pay review tied to the release I led.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be fairly calm about my job, but the empty savings account nags at me. A cancelled contract could empty our rent account before AI changes my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sam about the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Sam (my partner) we can keep the flat, but skip the winter trip until the cushion reaches one month of rent. That conversation would be about our cash, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in front of your manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show my manager the bugs our team caught after the assistant wrote tests. I’d ask for a raise with that evidence, though I cannot count on getting one.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave our hard debugging work largely where it is.
I’d tell customers we can **save time** on routine tests without promising miracles.
think: I’m **relieved** the job remains, yet a lost contract could still put rent at risk.
My **thin savings** matter more than the software in this picture.
do: **Keep** leading bug reviews and use the assistant for small tests.
**Save** 40 a month from my next pay, even if the goal takes time.
**Ask** for a release-based pay review during the first year.
feel: **Calm** about the work, with a nagging worry about rent.
S0.quote: A cancelled contract could empty our rent account before AI changes my job.
fieldNote: Her public line is **measured** because she already uses the tool daily and knows its limits.
The **rent cushion** is her immediate worry; she plans a small monthly saving and a conditional pay request.

steps.text: Keep leading bug reviews and using the coding assistant for small tests
Move 40 from each pay into rent savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I’d say Steady Disruption means our first drafts will get faster, and we should show what humans still catch. I would push for training time, not a quiet reduction in headcount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my lead title may protect me less than people think. If the assistant handles coding and test writing, the company may decide four developers can become two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d measure which faults the assistant misses and teach the team to review them. I’d ask management for paid time to learn system design and security, and I’d save 80 a month if our rent budget allows. If staff reductions begin in the first year, I’d join our local developers’ association to press for notice before cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious, even while I enjoy the new tools. I can picture doing better work and still receiving a smaller team roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my junior colleague Lina that reviews and customer conversations count, then pair with her on a production fault. I can’t promise her a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if management refuses paid learning time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my manager says training has no budget, I’d use one evening a week for the free security course. I would not pay for a certificate while our savings are so thin.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed up drafts while leaving careful reviews valuable.
I’d seek **training time** and clear notice before any staff cuts.
think: My **lead title** may not save me if management cuts the four-person team.
I like the tools, but a **smaller team** could cost junior colleagues their jobs.
do: **Measure** faults missed by AI and train colleagues to review them this month.
**Request** paid security and system-design learning; use a free course if refused.
**Join** the local developers’ association if staff reductions begin.
feel: **Anxious** about possible cuts, while genuinely interested in better tools.
S1.quote: I can picture doing better work and still receiving a smaller team roster.
fieldNote: She frames **quality evidence** as a way to defend jobs, yet expects management may still cut staff.
Her **training request** depends on company funding; she has a free course as a fallback.

steps.text: Track coding assistant faults and teach the team to review them
Ask for paid security training or take a free evening course
Join the developers association if staff cuts begin

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 is a serious threat to software jobs, and that we need honest staffing plans. Thinking AI would reach our code and design in 2028; robots arriving around 2031 would not give our desk work extra protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think implementation work at my company could nearly vanish by 2028. My company could keep one customer contact, but I cannot gamble the rent on being chosen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I’d put 80 a month aside if we can spare it and ask Sam to make a three-month emergency budget with me. I’d apply for product support roles at firms with real customers, even if the pay is similar. In the first year after 2028, if my role disappears, I’d take temporary support work and apply for available income help while I search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed. I can make a plan on paper, but two years is too short to build a real buffer from this wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which expense changes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first cut would be meals out and the winter trip, not Sam’s bus pass to work. Our rent is fixed, so the small choices only buy weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the company for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager for written notice and paid transition time. If the company cannot fund it, I’d take the support job first and study in the evenings; I would not borrow for a new degree.

say: I think **AGI by 2028** threatens software staffing as soon as thinking work becomes cheaper.
I’d ask for **written plans** on staffing and paid transition time.
think: My company may keep one **customer contact** while dropping much of the coding team.
My **rent** cannot depend on being the one person retained.
do: **Save** 80 monthly if the household budget permits, and plan three months of essential costs.
**Apply** now for product support roles with customer contact.
**Seek** temporary support work and available income help if my job ends after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely lost income and too little time to build a cushion.
S2.quote: My company could keep one customer contact, but I cannot gamble the rent on being chosen.
fieldNote: She distinguishes the **2028 thinking shift** from robots due around 2031; desk work faces the earlier date.
Her **fallback** requires a vacancy and possible public help; she will not finance another degree with debt.

steps.text: Set aside 80 monthly if rent leaves room
Apply for product support roles with customer contact
Apply for available income help if the developer job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d call AGI by 2031 a deadline for reshaping the team, not an excuse for panic today. Our code work would change in 2031; the robots due around 2034 hardly matter to our desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to become good at deciding what a product should do, but it does not guarantee an employer will pay for that skill. I’d still worry that a cheaper system will do the planning too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask to spend one day each month with customer support and record the problems users actually report. I’d take a low-cost course in accessibility design over the next year and save 80 a month if possible. In the first year after 2031, I’d try for a product role at my firm, and apply elsewhere if there is no opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, though I can breathe more easily than in the two-year picture. Five years would let me show customer problems I solved on a product-job application.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you prove that new skill at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d bring my manager a short record of the customer problems I solved, not a promise that AI cannot do them. If there is no funded path at work, I’d spend my own limited course money only on the low-cost option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a longer timeline change your housing plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam and I would keep the current flat until we had at least three months of rent saved. I would not sign a larger lease merely because the date feels farther away.

say: I think **AGI by 2031** gives our team time to change roles deliberately.
I see the **2034 robots** as less relevant to our desk-based work.
think: I worry product decisions may also become **cheap** by 2031, so a new title offers no guarantee.
I could build **evidence** of customer work in five years before applying.
do: **Shadow** customer support monthly and keep a record of user problems.
**Study** accessibility design through a low-cost course this year and save 80 monthly if possible.
**Apply** for a product role after 2031, elsewhere if my firm has no opening.
feel: **Anxious**, with more room to prepare than under the 2028 timeline.
S3.quote: Five years would let me show customer problems I solved on a product-job application.
fieldNote: She treats **five years** as usable time for evidence, not proof that product jobs survive.
Her **housing restraint** and course spending reflect less than a month of savings.

steps.text: Take a low-cost accessibility design course this year
Apply for a product role after 2031 if one is available
Save 80 monthly toward three months of rent when possible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to prepare, and I’d want the company to share the gains with staff. The thinking work changes in 2036, while hands-on robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a broader career by then, but ten years is also long enough for the company to keep wages low while calling every cut preparation. I do not want to spend my thirties chasing a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d negotiate a proper lead salary with evidence from our releases, then keep a monthly savings transfer if I get it. I’d volunteer to meet customers quarterly and take the company’s accessibility training if funded. In the first year after 2036, I’d choose between product leadership and another employer based on actual openings and pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mostly because low pay could keep my rent at risk while everyone postpones fair pay. I feel capable of changing my work over a decade, provided I can afford to stay in the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the salary request fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the raise fails, I’d still save what I can, but 80 every month would be wishful thinking. I’d search for a better-paid lead job beyond our town before paying for more training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair company plan include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for a training budget and a written internal path into product work. I would support colleagues asking together for notice and a share of the savings if AI reduces headcount.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as a decade to build skills and negotiate fairly.
I’d ask the company to **share gains** and give staff clear notice.
think: I worry a long timeline could let management **delay pay** while talking about future change.
I can probably shift roles if the work comes with **livable pay**.
do: **Negotiate** lead pay using release results this year.
**Meet** customers quarterly and take funded accessibility training if offered.
**Seek** a better-paid lead role if my salary request fails.
feel: **Anxious** about low pay and rent, though able to plan over ten years.
S4.quote: I do not want to spend my thirties chasing a promise.
fieldNote: Her **decade** supports a broader career plan, while present low pay remains the immediate constraint.
She conditions any **savings transfer** on getting a raise and would search elsewhere if refused.

steps.text: Keep leading releases while seeking a proper lead salary
Take company accessibility training if it is funded
Search for a better-paid lead role if the raise fails

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. A written staffing plan, paid time to move into customer work, and income help if the job ends would make the difference. I cannot build three months of rent from this salary in two years by skipping coffee.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the savings when software does more of the work. My team can adapt, but adaptation has a price, and right now the workers are paying it.

headlineQuote: My team can adapt, but adaptation has a price, and right now the workers are paying it.
portrait: Zoe is a **27-year-old lead developer** with a master’s degree, strong debugging skills and daily use of AI coding tools.
Her **low pay** and savings below one month make rent fragile despite her senior role and partner’s bookshop income.
She welcomes useful tools but fears **staff cuts** when thinking AI reaches software work, especially by 2028.
She seeks **customer-facing skills**, evidence of quality and collective notice, with plans limited by funding and actual vacancies.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her coding role before she can save three months of rent.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing plan**, paid transition time and income help if her job ends would help.
